ground_truth: When I was 30 years old, I was several times a millionaire. I knew it, but I can remember, as an example, it wasn't very important to me. I remember saying to my administrative assistant, do I have any money? She says, why do you ask? I said, because I want to buy a car. She says, well, of course you have money. How much do you want to spend on a car? Maybe I said it was $3,000, so yeah, no question, you could afford that. How I kept score was the growth of the business, but it wasn't about score in terms of how much money I was making. I felt good about what I was doing. I knew I was employing people. I was growing the business. It was just tons of fun. I think it's probably analogous to how an athlete would feel that just enjoys the sport and the fact that you get paid. I think Tiger Woods loves playing golf and he loves winning. The fact that he got paid just made it all the better. I think that the retail game, I tell my kids this, I tell people that I'm recruiting, it's just wonderful because it's all about people. If you like accounting, you can do accounting. If you want to do money in banking, you can do money in banking. There's a tasteful part that comes in the selection of merchandise, store design, systems design, so everything, all aspects of business come together in retailing. It's really tough because it's relentless. We're not building jet engines. We're guessing what young women are going to want to buy next week and three months from now. The fickle fashion, the challenge of it, you have to be in the game every day because it's changing. We don't have a book of orders like GE does making jet engines. They design a new one every decade and the order book lasts for three years.

ground_truth: I go, I'm there for the opening and pre-opening and design and setting up the store and about a block away there's a small lingerie store and the ladies in the store say, you have to go see it. But it was interesting and I just never had seen anything. I called the owner up, found out who the owner was, and I called him and I said, gee, next time I'm in San Francisco, I'd like to meet you. And he said, well, what do you do? And I told him I had the store down the street and he said, oh, I don't want to meet you because if I, you just want to understand my secrets and, you know, you'd probably want to start a business and put me out of business. I said, no, I'm just curious, which I was, and about a year later I get a phone call and the guy says, this is Roy Raymond. Remember, we had the phone conversation, I said, oh, yeah. And he said, are you still in, would you be interested in buying my business? So it was his idea, not mine. And I said, well, I don't know, I just, I didn't, you know, been thinking about lingerie business, haven't done anything, we're very busy doing things. And he said, well, if you want to buy it, you could buy it, but you have to come right away. And I said, well, maybe I'll be out in a week or two. He said, no, I'm, I'm, the sheriff's going to shut me down tomorrow, so if you want to buy the business, you've got to come out right now. So I said, okay, and just went out and met him, first time I met him, he told me about his business. He'd started it as a master's project, the way, not unlike the way Fred Smith started Federal Express, and he was going broke. And he had had no experience, he just, this was a 3D real life model of what he had written about in his master's project when he was at Stanford. And I said, it makes sense that, you know, people buy lingerie, I didn't know what the margin was, I didn't know anything about it, didn't know about fits, constructions, all this stuff. I said, I'll, I'd figure it out. And so bought the business. And we were a public company. I didn't know anything about it. We were a public company. I called our board and I said, well, I bought this business, and the response was, well, everybody can have a toy. So, you know, if this is something you want to play with, it's okay, but it could never be a business. So that was kind of daunting. And we were very busy with other businesses. So just Ray, you know, Roy rather, we won't bother you, you know, well, here's some cash so you can pay your bills, just run the business and, you know, we'll talk every three months. I didn't. I was engaged. But the real risky businesses we bought, you can grow a business by starting a business, starting other businesses. You could buy a smaller business or you could acquire a larger business. And one Friday morning I was looking at the Wall Street Journal and it said the management of a company called Lane Bryant was going to buy the company. And I thought, gee, this is kind of interesting. If it's a public company and the people that are running the company are going to buy the company. And the company had tried to sell itself and there weren't any buyers, so the management of the company decided they were going to buy it. Well, if that's a good deal for them, it might be a good deal for us. Got some public information, called the president of the company and said, well, we want to bid. And he said, well, you have to, you know, I'm running the company and I'm a bidder, so, you know, fry ice. And then we called their lawyer. Who was? Who was mentioned in the paper said, you know, the company lawyer said, we're real bidders and went to New York on a Friday afternoon, got a little bit of information about how many stores and how much business they've done, no financials. Met with manufacturers, Hannover Trust, on a Saturday morning and arranged for a loan, bid on the company and Monday night we owned it. So I get home around 3 in the morning from New York, and the net worth of the business was about, our business was about $120 million. We borrowed $150 million from Manufacturers Hanover to buy Lane Bryant. The story was, I get home, I'm back at my house in Columbus, I go in the refrigerator, it's 3 in the morning, pour myself a big glass of white wine, and I remember looking in the window and seeing my reflection and sipping the wine and saying, you've just bet the ranch.
